changes.before: Not a moratorium. Regulates "large energy use facilities" through RCA-approved utility contracts, cost-causation rules, long-term service commitments, direct assignment of facility-driven utility costs, and municipal community benefit agreements before contract approval. The introduced threshold is 20 MW peak electric demand or 20 percent of prior-year utility sales, and 2 billion standard cubic feet of gas annually or 20 percent of prior-year gas sales.
changes.after: Not a moratorium. The introduced bill would regulate "large energy use facilities" through RCA-approved utility contracts, cost-causation rules, long-term service commitments, direct assignment of facility-driven utility costs, and municipal community benefit agreements before contract approval. The introduced threshold is 20 MW peak electric demand or 20 percent of prior-year utility electricity sales, or 2 billion standard cubic feet of gas annually or 20 percent of prior-year gas sales, whichever is smaller for gas. The contract section excludes utility service to another public utility.

changes.before: Not a moratorium. Directly regulates data centers and utility service. The committee substitute requires data centers to pay facility-driven utility costs, provide financial security for utility capital investments above $1 million, use contracts that avoid fuel-supply and reliability risk shifting, include backup power and reliability planning, execute municipal CBAs, address waste heat, water use, broadband interconnection, digital equity, and file decommissioning and recycling plans. The committee substitute exempts data centers consuming both less than 15 MW peak electric demand and less than 1.5 billion standard cubic feet of gas annually.
changes.after: Not a moratorium. The committee substitute would directly regulate data centers and utility service. It would require data centers to pay facility-driven utility costs, provide financial security for utility capital investments above $1 million, use contracts that avoid fuel-supply and reliability risk shifting, include backup power and reliability planning, execute municipal CBAs, address waste heat, water use, broadband interconnection, digital equity, and file decommissioning and recycling plans. The proposed contract and decommissioning sections do not apply to data centers consuming both less than 15 MW peak electric demand from an electric utility and less than 1.5 billion standard cubic feet of gas annually; the separate utility cost-recovery provision does not state that exemption.

changes.before: The Town Board of the Town of South Fork introduced and passed Emergency Ordinance No. 2026-03 on June 18, 2026, per the archived legal notice published in the Valley Courier's July 1, 2026 edition. changes.after: The July 1, 2026 Valley Courier published Ordinance No. 2026-03 under a Town of South Fork heading and states that it passed and was signed June 18, 2026. Its introduction names the Town of Center; the discrepancy remains unresolved.

changes.after: Published Emergency Ordinance No. 2026-03 identifies South Fork in its heading and operative text, but names the Town of Center in its introduction; jurisdictional attribution requires clarification.

changes.before: Pauses submission, acceptance, processing, review, hearings, approval, and siting of new or expanded data centers while the city develops definitions and land-use, water, and wastewater rules. The city's posted first-reading document (posted June 19, 2026, before the amendment) still shows the pre-amendment 12-month figure and blank termination-date placeholders; a signed second-reading ordinance with the filled-in date was not located, but the 18-month figure is independently corroborated by Colorado Newsline and the Denver Gazette.

changes.before: Active as of 2026-09-23. The Town Council unanimously adopted Resolution TC31-65 on 2026-09-09, imposing a 2-year moratorium (effective immediately) on the 'establishment and development' of any new data centers in Trumbull. The moratorium does NOT apply to the modernization/upgrade of the town's existing 80 Merritt Blvd. data center (a 15 MW facility in operation 50+ years, now being converted to AI-ready use by 365 Data Centers), which the town characterizes as a renovation rather than new construction; residents have petitioned unsuccessfully to have that project included and are considering a signature drive (requiring roughly 2,400 voters) to force a referendum.

changes.before: Pending as of 2026-09-23. The draft ordinance would immediately suspend the City's acceptance, processing, review, approval, and issuance of permits, site plan approvals, conditional-use approvals, rezonings, subdivision approvals, building permits, utility service agreements, and certificates of occupancy for any new 'Large Energy Use Facility' (a facility using 75+ MW at 85%+ load factor, 100+ MW instantaneous demand, or 30+ MW and NAICS 518210) for 18 months, with exemptions for government/hospital/university/public-safety/clean-hydrogen facilities and small expansions. First proposed publicly in August 2026 (a City Council committee voted unanimously to advance a draft to full Council); the Council Committee of the Whole heard the finalized ordinance text on 2026-09-15 and recommended it go to full Council and the Planning Commission, but no first or final reading before full Council, and no ordinance number, had been recorded as of 2026-09-23. A sponsor's public social-media post described the proposal as a 24-month moratorium, which conflicts with the 18-month term stated in the drafted ordinance text reviewed here; the ordinance text is treated as authoritative.
changes.after: Pending as of 2026-09-23. First proposed publicly in August 2026 (a City Council committee voted unanimously to advance a draft to full Council); the Council Committee of the Whole heard the finalized ordinance text on 2026-09-15 and recommended it go to full Council and the Planning Commission, but no first or final reading before full Council, and no ordinance number, had been recorded as of 2026-09-23.
